# Agent Workbench [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/agent-workbench)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/agent-workbench) [![CI](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![license: MIT](https://img.shields.io/npm/l/agent-workbench)](LICENSE) [![Mentioned in Awesome Claude Code](https://awesome.re/mentioned-badge.svg)](https://github.com/hesreallyhim/awesome-claude-code) **English** · [Español](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.es.md) · [简体中文](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.zh-CN.md) · [日本語](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.ja.md) · [Português (Brasil)](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.pt-BR.md) · [Русский](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.ru.md) · [한국어](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.ko.md) · [Français](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.fr.md) · [Deutsch](https://github.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/blob/main/README.de.md) **A visual workbench for the coding agents you already use: the Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity and Pi CLIs.** It runs on your computer and opens in your browser. It uses the CLIs you already have installed and logged in, never touches your credentials, and makes no network calls of its own. ```bash npx agent-workbench ``` ![A tour: the conversation as cards, the changed files and a diff, one tab per CLI, and continuing a conversation with another CLI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/main/assets/demo.webp) ▶ **[Video tutorial](https://youtu.be/C0Iea1cKQ7o)**: the whole app in 6 minutes, with chapters to jump straight to what you need. [Official YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCVnU5e6NnF9xVSCRhy_UJQA): tutorials and demos. ## How it works Agent Workbench doesn't talk to any AI service. It starts the CLI you already have —`claude`, `codex`, `opencode`, `agy` or `pi`— inside a real terminal, and adds around it what a terminal alone doesn't give you: tabs, your past conversations, the conversation as easy-to-read cards, a context meter, the files that changed and a file tree. The terminal is still the terminal: everything you type goes straight to the CLI. --- ## What you get | | | |---|---| | **Tabs** | Several agents at once, from any CLI, each in its own folder. A dot on each tab tells you whether the agent is working, idle or waiting for you. Reloading the page doesn't stop anything: the CLIs run on the server, not in the browser. | | **Fast start** | When you open the app, your tabs come back **asleep**: you can read them in full, and no CLI starts until you click **Open CLI**. | | **History** | Your projects and past conversations in the sidebar, from every CLI, with a filter. Click one to pick it up where you left it, with its CLI. Archive old sessions or a whole project to tidy up: nothing is deleted, and it can be undone. | | **Conversation** | The messages as cards, live, with tool calls folded. Older messages load as you scroll up. Search, copy any message or code block, and jump back to your previous message (↑) or to the end (↓). A row at the bottom says when your message reached the CLI and whether the agent is still working. Depending on the CLI, you can answer the agent's questions right there. A file of the project that the agent names opens in the Files tab with one click, and a folder, in the system's file explorer. With Claude Code, a message you stop before the agent starts comes back to the box so you can fix it, and **↩** on a message goes back to before it: the conversation and, if you want, the code. A message you send while the agent works waits at the end, marked as queued; depending on the CLI, **Force send now** makes the agent read it right away, and **Edit** (or ↑ in the empty box) brings it back to the box to fix it. | | **Message box** | Room to write, paste images, attach files, and long pasted text kept as a tidy chip. What you're typing survives closing the app, and shows up live in every open window. Shift+Enter continues a numbered or bulleted list. Native voice controls offer dictation with Claude Code, live conversation with Codex, and both with Antigravity CLI, depending on the installed CLI version. Dictated text returns to the box for you to review and send. The clock sends what you wrote on its own, on the day and at the time you choose, in the same conversation; turn it on in Settings (Antigravity CLI needs its status line). | | **Context meter** | How much of the model's context window the conversation is using. Tokens, never money. Hover over or focus the meter to reveal **Compact**; from 70% it stays visible. It asks the CLI to compact the conversation. Next to it, with Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity CLI, how much of your plan's usage limits you've used and when they reset. | | **Changes** | The branch, the changed files and their diff. **Orchestrates agents in parallel**: open the project on a new branch, in its own folder, and several agents work at once without stepping on each other's changes. A conversation already under way moves to a new branch too, with all its context (with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode). Changes shows every branch: what isn't committed yet, how many commits it has and whether it's merged. Another CLI reviews a branch without touching it, and you merge it into main with one click. | | **Files** | The project's file tree, with search and a preview with syntax highlighting. Open several files at once, each in its own tab; Markdown files open formatted. One click puts a file's path in your message. Edit a text file, a `.env` for instance, and save it right there: if the agent changed it while you were editing, nothing is overwritten, and you move your changes to the new version. | | **Plans** | The plans and `.md` documents the conversation wrote, rendered. One click puts a document's path in your message. | | **Notes** | A scratchpad next to the conversation, with images and file attachments you can download. Shift+Enter continues a numbered or bulleted list. **To message box** puts the note and its attachments in the message box, to send them to the conversation you're in; with Claude Code, one click sends it to a new one. | | **Console** | Your system's terminal at the bottom, in the project's folder: PowerShell, cmd or Git Bash on Windows; bash or zsh on macOS and Linux. On a phone, the CLI has Enter and 1, 2, 3 for menus, and the console has extra navigation and editing keys. | | **Continue with…** | With more than one CLI, continue a conversation with another one in the same folder. The new agent starts from a transcript of the last turns, with instructions to preserve completed work, referenced plans and pending approvals. The continuation stays editable in the message box so you can add instructions and choose the model before sending. Conversations kept only in the backup, or belonging to a relocated project, can also continue with the same CLI in a new session. | | **Notifications** | A sound, and optional system notifications, when an agent finishes or is waiting for you. | | **Settings** | ⚙ in the header: the language, the terminal's theme, which panels show, which console opens, which CLIs the app uses and whether you can schedule messages. | | **Nine languages** | English, Español, 简体中文, 日本語, Português (Brasil), Русский, 한국어, Français and Deutsch. It follows your browser's language. | | **Theme** | Light, dark or the system's. The terminal stays dark by default, so the CLIs' colors stay readable. | With Codex, the conversation also offers model and permission controls, plans, and cards for recognized command approvals, file edits, terminal input, MCP tools, plan choices and questions, including in narrow terminals. Available controls depend on your Codex version; unrecognized menus stay in the CLI. Antigravity CLI supports images, question cards, plans and Markdown artifacts, and shows running subagents. Claude Code suggestions can be accepted in the message box. Voice uses the CLI's own audio support on the computer running it. Hold the dictation button, or Space for a second in the message box, to start dictating; live conversation has its own control. Agent Workbench does not record audio or transcribe it itself. Optional, and off by default: [shared memory](#shared-memory-between-clis) between CLIs, a [backup](#backup-of-your-history) of your history, Claude Code's [plan usage limits](#claude-code-plan-usage-limits), [remote access](#remote-access-over-ssh) from another computer or a phone, and an [Android app](#the-android-app).

### With more than one CLI Each session and each tab shows a small badge with its CLI, and the `+` for a new tab lets you pick which one to open. With a single CLI you see none of this. **Not every CLI shares the same information**, so a few features depend on the CLI: | | Claude Code | Codex | OpenCode | Antigravity CLI | Pi | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:| | Tab dot: working, idle, waiting for you | ✓ | — | ✓ ¹ | ✓ ² | ✓ | | Answer the agent's questions from the conversation | ✓ | ✓ ⁴ | ✓ ¹ | ✓ | — | | Context meter | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ ² | ✓ | | Mode, model and reasoning effort pickers | ✓ | ✓ ⁴ | — | ✓ | ✓ ³ | | Voice dictation | ✓ ⁵ | - | - | ✓ ⁵ | - | | Live voice conversation | - | ✓ ⁴ ⁵ | - | ✓ ⁵ | - | | Paste images | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ ³ | | Plans tab | ✓ | ✓ | — | ✓ | — | | Send a note to a new conversation | ✓ | — | — | — | — | The CLI's own terminal is always there for the rest: where there's a "—", questions, for example, are answered in it. ¹ With OpenCode, the app starts a local OpenCode server to get this ([details](#your-data-and-security)). ² Only if you set up its status line ([how](#antigravity-cli-status-and-context-meter)). ³ Pi has no permission modes: its pickers are the model and the thinking level. And it doesn't attach what you paste: an image travels as a file path that the model opens itself. ⁴ Codex controls depend on the installed version. Question and approval cards cover recognized menus; the CLI's terminal remains available for the rest. Live voice conversation requires Codex 0.166 or newer. ⁵ Voice controls are available locally on the computer running the CLI, using its microphone and speakers. Availability depends on the CLI's version and setup. --- ## Requirements - **Node.js 20 or later.** To see OpenCode's history and Antigravity CLI's conversation titles, **22.13 or later**: they're read with the SQLite built into Node since that version. With an older one, everything else works. - **git**, for the Changes panel. Everything else works without it. - **At least one CLI**, installed and logged in: | CLI | Command | How to install | |---|---|---| | Claude Code | `claude` | [installation guide](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/setup) | | Codex | `codex` | [guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli) | | OpenCode | `opencode` | [documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/) | | Antigravity CLI | `agy` | [guide](https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/getting-started) | | Pi | `pi` | [pi.dev](https://pi.dev) | Agent Workbench doesn't include or download any CLI: it finds the ones in your `PATH`. If there are none, it tells you so and doesn't open sessions. **Platforms.** Built and used every day on Windows 11 with PowerShell. On macOS and Linux, every change is installed and started automatically, but they get less daily use: reports are welcome. On Linux, installing compiles the terminal module, so you need `python3`, `make` and a C++ compiler (`build-essential` on Debian and Ubuntu). --- ## Install and start ```bash npm install -g agent-workbench ``` Then, from the folder of the project you want to work on: ```bash agent-workbench ``` It opens your browser at an address like this one: ``` URL http://127.0.0.1:52341/?token=… ``` That address is the only way in: the token changes on every start, and the app only listens on your own computer (`127.0.0.1`). To try it once without installing: `npx agent-workbench`. It downloads about 60 MB the first time, mostly the terminal's native module. For everyday use, the global install is better. --- ## Keyboard shortcuts | Keys | Action | |---|---| | `Alt+T` | New tab | | `Alt+W` | Close the tab | | `Alt+←` / `Alt+→` (or `Alt+PgUp` / `Alt+PgDn`) | Previous / next tab | | `Alt+P` | Show or hide the right panel | | `Shift+Tab`, outside the terminal | Back to the previous tab | The `?` button in the header lists them all, along with the active CLI's own shortcuts. They use `Alt` because the browser keeps `Ctrl+T`, `Ctrl+W` and `Ctrl+Tab` for its own tabs and never passes them to the page. Every other key —`Esc`, `Ctrl+C`, `Ctrl+R`, `Ctrl+O`, the arrows, `Alt+V` to paste images— reaches the CLI untouched. `Ctrl+V` too: what it does there is up to the CLI. Only in the console at the bottom, on Windows, `Ctrl+V` pastes text, as in Windows Terminal. --- ## Optional extras ### Shared memory between CLIs Each CLI keeps what it learns about a project in its own place, and the others can't see it. The **Memory** tab sets up one memory for all of them: notes in the project's `.agents/memory/` folder, which every CLI reads and writes from here or from its own terminal through `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. With no saved preference, the tab is visible when more than one CLI is available; otherwise, show it from ⚙ Settings. Setting up shared memory remains optional. **Preview changes** shows, file by file, what would be written, and nothing is touched until you confirm. Setting it up imports the memory Claude Code already had for that project. The app doesn't edit each CLI's global settings: it gives you the snippet to paste yourself. ### Backup of your history Each CLI owns its history, and it can change its format, prune it, or be uninstalled. The backup keeps a copy of your conversations —messages, tool calls and results, images, and each project's memory— in a folder of yours, in files you can read without the app. **It's off by default.** Open it with the backup button at the top of the projects sidebar, or from ⚙ Settings. **Measure** tells you how much space it would take per CLI, without writing anything, and **Turn on** starts it. From then on it copies everything in the sidebar that isn't archived, and copies a conversation again a minute after it stops changing. It never deletes anything from that folder. With the backup on: - Conversations a CLI no longer has stay in the sidebar, marked as backup, and open as Markdown. - Any project can be exported to Markdown. - With more than one CLI, the sidebar filter can search **In conversations**: the text of everything copied, from every CLI. ![A file from the tree, previewed with syntax highlighting](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cvelasquez/agent-workbench/main/assets/captura-archivos.png) --- ## Troubleshooting **"The "claude" command wasn't found in the PATH", followed by "Also works with: …"** — the app didn't find any of the CLIs. Check with `where claude` on Windows (`which claude` elsewhere), and the same with `codex`, `opencode`, `agy` or `pi`. CLIs are looked up at startup: if you installed one while the app was open, restart it. **Pi is installed, but the app doesn't see it.** The app doesn't run `pi` to find it: it reads the version from Pi's package, next to the command. That works when Pi was installed with npm or with the pi.dev installer; a standalone `pi` binary isn't recognized. And if another program called `pi` comes first in your `PATH`, the app ignores it and says so in its console. **In a Pi tab, the message box says the CLI is waiting for an answer.** Pi is asking whether to trust the project folder. Answer it in the **CLI** tab: the app never answers that for you. **OpenCode's history doesn't show up.** Look at the `History` line when the app starts. If it says that Node version doesn't include `node:sqlite`, update Node to 22.13 or later. If there's no such line, it didn't find the database: it's at `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, or wherever `OPENCODE_DB` or `XDG_DATA_HOME` points. **An OpenCode tab won't open: "Couldn't start the OpenCode server".** The reason comes after the colon. If it isn't clear, open `opencode` in a regular terminal: if it doesn't start there either, the problem is that OpenCode installation. **An OpenCode tab says the server closed.** **Relaunch**, in the same bar, starts another server and reconnects the tab to the same session. **Claude Code's plan limits don't show.** If the meter offers **Configure**, follow [these steps](#claude-code-plan-usage-limits). If it says **no data**, the status line is set but hasn't published them yet: they come with each session's first response, and only with a subscription plan. **An Antigravity tab doesn't show its status or the meter.** Look at the `Status line` entry when the app starts, under the CLI. If it says it isn't configured, or that there's another one, follow [these steps](#antigravity-cli-status-and-context-meter). If you configured it and the CLI's terminal shows `Statusline Error`, `node` is most likely not in that session's `PATH`. **`node-pty` doesn't compile on install.** It's the terminal's native module. It usually downloads a ready-made binary; if your Node and platform don't have one, it has to be compiled: - **Windows:** Visual Studio Build Tools with the *Desktop development with C++* workload, and Python 3. (`windows-build-tools` from npm is no longer maintained.) - **macOS:** `xcode-select --install`. - **Linux:** `build-essential` and `python3`. **The terminal stays blank.** The default renderer is canvas on purpose: with WebGL the tab freezes on Windows 11 + Chrome. To try WebGL anyway, add `?renderer=webgl` to the address. **A banner says `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION` was removed.** You started the app from inside a Claude Code session. That variable turns off history saving, so the app removes it and lets you know. From a regular terminal you'll never see this. **From the other computer, `ssh` can't connect** (it times out or is refused). The SSH server isn't running on the computer with the app, or something between the two blocks it. On Windows, check that the Wi‑Fi network is set to *Private*: the SSH server's firewall rule may not cover *Public* networks. A work VPN that blocks the local network also cuts it while it's connected. If `ssh` rejects your user, a Microsoft or work account may need the name of your user folder (`C:\Users\`) and the account's password, not the PIN. **From the other computer, the page says "Origin not allowed"** (403). It was opened by the computer's name or IP address. Open `http://localhost:`, with the tunnel using the same port on both ends. **From the other computer, the page says the session token is missing** (401). That browser isn't paired, it was revoked, or remote access is off. Pair it again from the ⇄ dialog. **The ⇄ dialog says the port is busy.** Another program —often a second Agent Workbench— is using it. Close it and restart, or choose another port. **The Changes panel says the folder isn't a git repository**, and it is one. Make sure `git` is in the `PATH`. If the message is a different one, it's git's own error, word for word. --- ## From source To work on the app, or if you'd rather not install anything globally: ```bash corepack enable pnpm pnpm install pnpm dev # with hot reload ``` ```bash pnpm build # builds the interface once pnpm start # serves the built interface ``` **One-click start on Windows:** `pnpm package` builds the interface and leaves an **`Agent Workbench.cmd`** in the root. Double-click it: it installs whatever is missing, builds if needed and opens the browser. It's a twenty-line text file you can read before running it. --- ## How it's built A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout. ``` packages/ server/ Node, Express, ws, node-pty, chokidar — serves the interface and runs the terminals src/agents/ one adapter per CLI: the only part of the server that knows each one web/ Vite, React, xterm.js, highlight.js shared/ the protocol types, with no `any` at the edges android/ the Android app, in Kotlin: the SSH tunnel, the interface, the notifications ``` Two decisions shape the rest. **The terminals live on the server and the browser is just a window onto them**: closing or reloading the page doesn't kill a working session. And **the generic server doesn't name any CLI**: what it knows about each one —where it keeps things, how it's launched, what is read and what is never opened— lives in that CLI's adapter, and the interface shows each control based on what that CLI declares. [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md) has the hard rules and the code map, [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md) how to work on the repository, [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md) how to report a vulnerability, [`PRIVACY.md`](PRIVACY.md) what is collected (nothing), and [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md) what changed in each version. Code comments are in Spanish. The screenshots in this README come from `pnpm demo:shots`, on made-up data. --- ## Support the project If Agent Workbench is useful to you, consider supporting it: [Buy Me a Coffee](https://buymeacoffee.com/cvelasquez). The app suggests it once per version, in a strip you can close, and never again until the next one. --- ## License MIT. See [`LICENSE`](LICENSE). Agent Workbench is an independent project. It works with the Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity and Pi CLIs, but it is not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic, OpenAI, the OpenCode authors, Google or Earendil.
